analysis.one_liner: Bans commercial logging on federal public lands and shifts the money to forest restoration and worker retraining.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2001 with 112 cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ended the federal government's program of selling timber from national forests and other public lands to logging companies, with a two-year phase-out for existing contracts. It would have replaced logging with an ecological restoration program, offered retraining and income support to workers who lost their jobs, and made federal payments to rural counties with federal land permanent. It also let any citizen go to court to enforce the law.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently pay for a logging program the bill cites Forest Service and GAO findings as running at a large net loss; people who use the forests for recreation; and logging workers and their communities, who would get federally funded retraining, job-search and relocation allowances, and permanent continuation of rural county payments.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers, forest users, and rural timber workers

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits new timber sales and commercial logging on national forests, wildlife refuges, parks, and BLM lands, with a two-year phase-out for existing contracts, and provides compensation for terminated contracts.

The bill cites GAO reports finding that of the hundreds of millions spent annually on the Forest Service timber sales program, only a small fraction comes back to the Treasury, producing a large net loss to taxpayers.

It authorizes worker retraining grants, needs-related payments, and job-search and relocation allowances of up to $80 million, $80 million, and $120 million per year during and after the phase-out, funded from the existing timber-sale accounts.
It amends the Secure Rural Schools Act to make the education, road, and other payments to counties containing federal land permanent, rather than ending after 2006.

It funds a Natural Heritage Restoration Corps to restore degraded lands, plus up to $15 million a year to help homeowners near federal lands reduce the flammability of their houses, which the bill cites Forest Service research as the most effective wildfire protection.

analysis.who_pays: Timber companies lose access to federal timber, which the bill's findings say is under five percent of U.S. annual timber consumption, so mills shift to other supply sources. Taxpayers fund contract termination payments and the transition programs, though appropriations are capped at two-thirds of what the logging program had been costing.

drawbacks.text: Logging jobs in rural communities would end, and the retraining program offers transition money but no guarantee of comparable local employment; timber towns in the Pacific Northwest had already absorbed large mill closures in the 1990s.

Federal timber is a small share of national consumption but a meaningful share of supply in some local mill towns, so those local economies would bear the adjustment cost even as county payments continue.

The bill's fire provisions would restrict thinning to removing hazardous fuels without reducing the forest canopy, and opponents of logging bans argued this limits land managers' options for reducing fire risk, a live concern given the severe 2000 and 2002 fire seasons.
Terminating existing timber contracts early would require paying damages or settlements to purchasers under the Contract Disputes Act, a real upfront cost on top of the phase-out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is built as a managed transition rather than an abrupt shutdown: two-year phase-out, contract compensation, $80–120 million a year in worker retraining, permanent county payments, and lower total appropriations than the logging program it replaces. The honest trade-off is that it protects taxpayers and forests at the expense of a specific set of rural logging jobs, and its fire-protection approach was contested at a time of severe wildfire seasons.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and four subcommittees in April 2001, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Cynthia McKinney introduced the bill on April 4, 2001, and 112 members cosponsored it, including 109 of 208 House Democrats, 2 of 223 House Republicans, and the chamber's single Independent.
The Speaker referred it to the Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Education and the Workforce Committees, and it was then assigned to subcommittees; the committees never reported it out.
Executive comment was requested from the Departments of Agriculture and Interior, but no hearing or markup appears anywhere in the action history.
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and all bills not passed die at that point, so the logging ban was never considered by either chamber.
Federal commercial logging on public lands continued throughout the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The timber industry kept access to federal timber sales, and taxpayers continued funding a logging program the bill cited GAO reports as running at a net loss.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The timber industry and the logging program's status quo

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Democratic: 109 of 208 House Democrats and the sole Independent signed on, versus only 2 of 223 House Republicans, and the Republican-controlled committees never advanced the bill to a vote.

industries.note: The bill ends sales of federal timber, which the timber industry buys at prices that often do not cover the Forest Service's costs, a subsidy the bill's findings document as a large net loss to taxpayers. Federal timber is under five percent of U.S. consumption, so the loss is concentrated in the companies that relied on cheap public timber.

The bill's findings cite a Forest Service plan showing recreation and tourism generate over 30 times more jobs and income on national forests than logging does. Healthier, less road-cut forests support this growing economic use.

Logging and mill jobs would be lost, but the bill provides $80–120 million a year in retraining, job-search and relocation allowances, and makes the rural county payments under the Secure Rural Schools Act permanent, cushioning schools and roads funded by logging receipts.
